reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Acoustic neuroma is a benign, slow-growing schwannoma that usually arises from the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve, so vestibular schwannoma is the more accurate term
It typically presents with unilateral or asymmetrical sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, and any such asymmetry should prompt investigation
Speech discrimination is often disproportionately poor relative to the pure tone loss, a clue to a retrocochlear lesion
Balance disturbance is often mild because the slow growth allows central compensation, so vertigo is usually less prominent than expected
As the tumour enlarges within the cerebellopontine angle it can compress the trigeminal nerve, causing facial numbness and a reduced corneal reflex
Facial nerve function is usually preserved until late despite the nerve's proximity, and early facial weakness should raise doubt about the diagnosis
MRI with contrast of the internal auditory meatus is the gold standard investigation and detects even small intracanalicular tumours
Management is individualised between observation with serial imaging, stereotactic radiosurgery, and microsurgical excision, depending on size, growth, symptoms, hearing and age
reference.pathophysiology: Acoustic neuroma is a benign neoplasm of Schwann cells, most often originating at the transition zone of the vestibular nerve within or near the internal auditory canal. As it grows it first fills the canal, compressing the cochlear and vestibular fibres and their blood supply to produce sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. Continued expansion into the cerebellopontine angle displaces and stretches adjacent structures: the trigeminal nerve above, the facial nerve alongside, and eventually the brainstem and cerebellum. Large tumours can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and raise intracranial pressure. Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, while bilateral tumours are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2.
additionalDifferentials: Presbycusis or noise-induced asymmetrical hearing loss
Meningioma or other cerebellopontine angle tumour
Epidermoid or arachnoid cyst of the cerebellopontine angle
Vascular loop compression of the eighth nerve
additionalInvestigations: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle
Pure tone and speech audiometry to characterise asymmetry and poor discrimination
Auditory brainstem response testing where MRI is contraindicated
Vestibular testing such as caloric responses
CT of the temporal bone in selected cases to assess bony anatomy for surgery
redFlags: Unilateral or asymmetrical sensorineural hearing loss or tinnitus mandating MRI to exclude the tumour
Facial numbness or an absent corneal reflex suggesting trigeminal involvement by a larger tumour
Headache, ataxia, vomiting or altered consciousness suggesting brainstem compression or raised intracranial pressure (an emergency)
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss, which can occasionally be the presenting feature
Bilateral tumours or a family history suggesting neurofibromatosis type 2
reference.prognosis: Because the tumour is benign and usually slow growing the prognosis is generally good, and small tumours may simply be observed; treatment outcomes depend on tumour size at diagnosis, with hearing preservation and facial nerve function being more achievable when tumours are small.
pitfalls: Attributing unilateral hearing loss or tinnitus to age or noise without imaging
Overlooking disproportionately poor speech discrimination as a retrocochlear clue
Assuming prominent vertigo must be present, when balance symptoms are often mild
Missing the significance of facial numbness or an absent corneal reflex
Failing to consider neurofibromatosis type 2 in young or bilateral cases
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Active surveillance with serial gadolinium-enhanced MRI for small, minimally symptomatic or slow-growing tumours
Stereotactic radiosurgery or radiotherapy such as gamma knife for small-to-medium tumours or where surgery is unsuitable, to arrest growth

Microsurgical excision by a translabyrinthine, retrosigmoid or middle-fossa approach for larger tumours or those compressing the brainstem, with intraoperative facial nerve monitoring and preservation
Management of hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure arising from large cerebellopontine-angle tumours
Audiological rehabilitation and hearing support for sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular rehabilitation for imbalance
Screen for and manage neurofibromatosis type 2 in bilateral tumours, including genetic counselling and consideration of bevacizumab
Skull-base multidisciplinary team follow-up spanning ENT and neurosurgery
